statement: In 9 healthy young men who had taken MDMA before (5 to 100 times; on average 26), MDMA (100 mg) taken with alcohol (0.8 g/kg), compared with each drug alone and with a dummy in the same men, one week apart, in random order under double-blind, double-dummy conditions in a quiet laboratory room (study conditions), was associated with feeling as drunk as with alcohol alone but less sleepy, with test scores that fell about as far at their worst as with alcohol alone, and with a little more MDMA and a little less alcohol in the blood (Hernández-López et al., 2002). Feelings: a sedation score rose with alcohol alone but not with both drugs, where it stayed at the level of MDMA alone, and drowsiness ratings were lower with both drugs than with alcohol alone; ratings of feeling drunk rose with alcohol alone and with both drugs, with no significant difference between the two (at their peak about 58 with both drugs and about 40 with alcohol alone on a 100 mm line, editors' reading of the figure), and the authors conclude that MDMA reversed alcohol's sedation but did not reduce drunkenness; ratings of feeling high and stimulated rose with MDMA and with both drugs. Tests: on a timed symbol-matching test (digit symbol substitution), correct answers at the worst point fell by 9.0 with alcohol alone and by 8.11 with both drugs against the dummy (no significant difference between the two), but with both drugs the fall lasted about 1 hour (1 to 2 hours after the capsule) against 2 to 3 hours with alcohol alone, and over 6 hours it did not differ significantly from the dummy; decision time in a reaction test was slower than with the dummy at its peak only with both drugs, for about half an hour. Blood levels: MDMA peaked 13% higher with alcohol (260.29 against 231.42; p = 0.007), with no change in total exposure, and alcohol peaked 15% lower with MDMA (105.81 against 124.62 mg/dl; p = 0.004) and was 9% lower over 6 hours; the authors call these changes mild and within the range of differences between people. The MDMA levels are printed in mg/dl, which cannot be right for these values: the assay's stated range (25 to 400 ng/ml) points to ng/ml. Heart and body: the paper says cardiovascular, hormone and other physiological measures were taken but are not presented, and cites no paper that reports them, so it says nothing about what the mix does to heart rate or blood pressure (body temperature is not named among the measures); no serious adverse reaction occurred and all 9 finished. Nobody was asked how well they thought they were doing, and nobody drove: the authors' suggestion that people may feel they are doing better, or drive recklessly, is untested, and they say driving and field studies are needed. The men were healthy, experienced with MDMA, without past bad reactions to it, all with normal activity of a liver enzyme (CYP2D6) that breaks MDMA down, and given one amount of each drug once; women, people new to MDMA, other amounts, repeated doses, heat, dancing and crowds were not studied. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: What happens when you mix MDMA with alcohol? In one lab study, 9 healthy men who had taken MDMA before each had four sessions a week apart: MDMA, alcohol, both, or neither, with dummy pills and drinks so they did not know which. With both, the sleepy feeling that alcohol brought went away, but feeling drunk did not: if anything it was rated a bit higher, though not clearly so. On a timed symbol test, scores at the worst point fell about as much as with alcohol alone, though for about 1 hour instead of 2 to 3, and only with both drugs was reaction time clearly slower than with the dummy. MDMA in the blood peaked 13% higher and alcohol 15% lower; the authors call these small changes. Heart measurements were taken but never reported, so the study says nothing about the heart. Nobody asked the men how well they thought they were doing, and nobody drove. It was 9 men, one amount of each drug, in a quiet room.
population: 9 healthy men aged 19 to 36 (mean 23) who had used MDMA recreationally on 5 to 100 occasions (mean 26) and had been drunk before, without past adverse reactions to MDMA or drug dependence other than nicotine (7 smoked), all extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers; recruited by word of mouth and paid; Barcelona
exposure: MDMA 100 mg (racemic, capsule, fasting) with alcohol 0.8 g/kg as vodka and tonic (350 ml drunk over 15 minutes, starting 30 minutes after the capsule), given double-blind and double-dummy in 10-hour outpatient sessions in a quiet room (study conditions, not advice)
comparator: The same men given MDMA with a placebo drink, a placebo capsule with alcohol, and both placebos, one week apart, in an order set by a balanced 4 × 4 Latin square
outcome: Digit symbol substitution test and simple reaction time (impairment as fewer responses or slower times than with placebo), eye-muscle balance (Maddox wing), self-rated sedation and other effects (ARCI) and 23 visual analogue scales including drunken and drowsiness, over 6 to 10 hours; blood MDMA and alcohol; cardiovascular and other physiological measures collected but not reported
magnitude: Hernández-López et al. (2002), 9 men; ANOVA df 3,24 with Tukey tests (Table 1). Sedation (ARCI-PCAG): area alcohol > placebo (p < 0.05) and > combination (p < 0.01), combination not different from placebo or MDMA; peak alcohol > combination (p < 0.05). Drowsiness: area alcohol > placebo and > combination (p < 0.01); peak alcohol > placebo (p < 0.01) and > combination (p < 0.05). Drunken: area and peak raised by alcohol and by the combination against placebo and MDMA (p < 0.01); alcohol against combination not significant; approximate peak ratings about 58 (combination) and 40 mm (alcohol alone), read from Fig. 3. Digit symbol substitution, mean peak differences against placebo: alcohol −5.89 total and −9.0 correct responses, combination −4.89 and −8.11 (peak p < 0.01 for both; alcohol against combination not significant); 6-h area: alcohol against placebo p < 0.01, combination not significant; impairment against placebo lasted 2–3 h with alcohol (from 1 h to 3–4 h) and 1 h with the combination (1–2 h). Reaction decision time, peak: combination against placebo p < 0.05, the only significant pair; the combination's impairment lasted half an hour (1–1.5 h). Euphoria and stimulation scales were raised by MDMA and the combination against placebo and alcohol (not compared here for strength or length). Blood levels (Table 2, mean ± SD; time to peak as median): MDMA peak 231.42 ± 36.20 alone and 260.29 ± 42.22 with alcohol, p = 0.007 (13% higher, the paper's figure), units printed as mg/dl but the assay range is 25–400 ng/ml, so ng/ml is likely; time to peak 1.5 h in both (p = 0.058); area 2447.85 ± 711.81 against 2345.08 ± 838.35, p = 0.471 (headed AUC0–6h, while the methods give AUC0–24h for MDMA, which was sampled only to 10 h). Alcohol peak 124.62 ± 14.94 alone and 105.81 ± 4.99 mg/dl with MDMA, p = 0.004 (15% lower); 6-h area 409.08 ± 24.28 against 371.74 ± 18.67, p < 0.001 (9% lower); time to peak 1.5 against 2 h (p = 0.014). No serious adverse reactions; all 9 completed. Cardiovascular, endocrine and other physiological measures were collected and not reported.

evidence.extracted: Nine healthy men recruited by word of mouth and paid, aged 23 on average (19–36), with recreational MDMA use on at least five occasions (mean 26, range 5–100) and earlier acute alcohol intoxication, no DSM-IV abuse or dependence except nicotine, no past adverse reactions to MDMA, all extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers; all but two smoked. Four conditions in a double-blind, double-dummy, randomized crossover (balanced 4 × 4 Latin square), one week apart, 10-h outpatient sessions seated in a quiet room: MDMA 100 mg plus alcohol 0.8 g/kg; MDMA plus placebo drink; placebo capsule plus alcohol; double placebo. The drink (vodka and tonic, 350 ml) was taken over 15 min starting 30 min after the capsules; the placebo drink was masked with bitters and lemon juice.

risk_of_bias.note: Randomized by a balanced Latin square (sequence generation and concealment not described; nine people cannot fill a 4 × 4 square evenly), double-dummy with a masked drink, but the experienced men were likely to recognise the conditions and the blind was not checked; drunkenness and sedation are self-ratings; no registration; cardiovascular and other physiological measures were collected and not reported, Table 1 lists only significant results, and the text goes beyond Table 1 in places (card sc_hernandez_lopez_2002: RoB 2 high overall, driven by selective reporting, which bears more on the unreported outcomes than on those described here). Test scores and blood levels are objective.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: 9 experienced men, one amount of each drug, laboratory tests of symbol matching and reaction time rather than driving or real-life impairment, which the statement says.

imprecision.note: 9 people; no standard deviations or intervals for the test and rating outcomes (means in figures only); the central comparisons, feeling as drunk and test scores falling as far as with alcohol alone, are non-significant differences that cannot show equality (the drunk ratings were numerically higher with both drugs), and the printed peak differences do not agree with one another (editors' check: they imply that MDMA alone differed from placebo by −0.89 and by 0 correct responses).

grade.reasoning: Randomized within-person crossover: starts high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias −1 and imprecision −2 give very low. The fall in self-rated sedation with both drugs against alcohol alone, and the changes in blood levels, are significant within-person differences and would be rated higher on their own; the claim's main point, that people felt as drunk and did about as badly on the test at its worst, rests on non-significant comparisons in 9 men. Status single study (the dose-finding pilot and the immune results from the same trial were not read). The claim gives risk facts only.

No paper reporting the trial's cardiovascular measures is cited. The brief's mention of temperature among the measures taken is not in the paper, which names cardiovascular, endocrine and other physiological parameters.
